pattern.crimePattern: co-heir kills the relative who refused to sell a family building
pattern.notes: Fictional family, shop and developer in a real Old Town street. Heritage-building pressure is a real theme; no real building or family is depicted.

ob.reportedBy: Rahma Abeid, shop assistant, Karimjee & Sons Spices, Ndia Kuu
ob.text: Rahma Abeid, a shop assistant, reports that her employer Farida Karimjee (64), owner of Karimjee & Sons Spices on Ndia Kuu, Old Town, was found dead in the shop at 16:25. A sack of turmeric is split across the floor.

people.name: Farida Karimjee
people.bio: Widow. Runs the spice shop her husband's grandfather opened, in a coral-stone building she will not sell.

image.brief: Kenyan Asian woman, mid 60s, grey hair in a low bun, a cotton salwar kameez with a cardigan, reading glasses, a scoop of cardamom in her hand, stubborn and kind, ID-photo framing

people.name: Yasmin Karimjee
people.occupation: Farida's sister-in-law; co-owner of the building
people.bio: Her late brother's share of the building came to her through the family trust. Short of money. Wants to sell.

image.brief: Kenyan Asian woman, mid 50s, a pale salwar suit with a long white dupatta that has a very faint yellow stain near one end, gold bangles, a tight controlled expression, ID-photo framing

people.name: Ken Mutisya
people.bio: Told Farida last week, in front of customers, "You'll sell, one way or another."

image.brief: Kenyan man, mid 40s, a slim grey suit, a lanyard from a county meeting, a tablet under his arm, smooth and impatient, ID-photo framing

people.name: Rahma Abeid
people.bio: Has worked in the shop for two years. Says she was there all afternoon.

image.brief: Swahili Kenyan young woman, early 20s, a navy hijab, a smart blouse a little too formal for a spice shop, a folded letter in her hand, frightened, ID-photo framing

people.name: Imran Karimjee
people.occupation: Farida's son, in Nairobi on business
people.bio: Unlocked his mother's phone for the police by video call.

people.name: Hussein Abdulkadir
people.bio: Carves doors on the pavement opposite. Sees everything on Ndia Kuu.

people.name: Ali Kitsao
people.bio: Drives between Ganjoni and Old Town.

locations.name: Karimjee & Sons Spices, Ndia Kuu
locations.description: A narrow shop in a coral-stone building with a carved wooden door. Open sacks of cumin, cardamom, cloves and chillies at the front. Behind the counter, a brass mortar and pestle. A sack of turmeric has split across the floor and the air is yellow with it.

hotspots.label: Behind the counter
hotspots.text: Farida lies behind the counter in a drift of turmeric. The brass pestle is beside her.

hotspots.label: The turmeric
hotspots.text: Bright yellow powder everywhere. In it, the smudged print of a flat sandal, pointing to the door.

hotspots.label: Phone on the counter
hotspots.text: Her phone, face down by the weighing scale. Imran unlocks it by video call from Nairobi.

hotspots.label: Counter drawer
hotspots.text: A drawer of letters. On top, a developer's letterhead.

hotspots.label: Under the letters
hotspots.text: A family trust deed in a plastic sleeve.

hotspots.label: Old ledger
hotspots.text: A cloth-bound family ledger, decades old.

hotspots.label: Bin
hotspots.text: Torn paper in the bin, typed.

hotspots.label: Cash box
hotspots.text: The cash box under the counter.

hotspots.label: Sales book
hotspots.text: Today's sales book, in Rahma's handwriting.

hotspots.label: Across the street
hotspots.text: Hussein Abdulkadir has put down his chisel and is standing in the street with his hands on his head.

evidence.title: Interview letter and hotel visitor book

body.letter: Interview, front office, hotel in Nyali, 16:00.

facts.text: Rahma Abeid found her employer Farida Karimjee dead in the spice shop at 16:25. Farida's son Imran is in Nairobi.
Farida was struck with the shop's brass pestle.
Turmeric stains cotton bright yellow and doesn't wash out. In the powder: a smudged print of a woman's flat sandal, heading to the door.
SMS to Farida from 'Yasmin' at 14:58: 'Nakuja saa tisa na nusu na karatasi' (I'm coming at half past three with the papers).
A developer's offer for the building: KSh 40 million. Across it, in Farida's hand: 'NEVER.'
Family trust deed: the building is held jointly by Farida and Yasmin, and a sale needs both signatures. The spice business is Farida's alone.
Torn in the bin: a typed 'consent to transfer' form for the building, unsigned.
Family ledger: an old loan from Farida to Yasmin, marked settled ten years ago.
The cash box is full: the day's takings counted and banded.
Sales book: no sales between 15:30 and 16:25 on a weekday afternoon.
Hussein: from about 15:35 the shop door was half closed with a sign, 'Narudi sasa hivi' (back shortly). Rahma came back at about 16:25 and screamed.
Hussein carved at his pavement workshop opposite the shop all afternoon.
Jamii Mobile, Yasmin's line: Ganjoni mast until 15:30, Old Town 15:42–16:14, Ganjoni again from 16:28.
PesaPap, Yasmin's line: tuk-tuk fares to ALI KITSAO at 15:38 and 16:12.
PesaPap, Yasmin's line, three days ago: KSh 15,000 to Till 880 214, MVUA HOLDINGS, 'title & transfer documents'.
Ali Kitsao: he dropped a woman in a white dupatta at the spice shop door on Ndia Kuu at about 15:47, and picked her up at the same door at 16:12. She sat on her feet.
Yasmin's white dupatta, washed today, still has faint yellow stains along one end.
Hotel visitor book, Nyali: R. Abeid, interview, in 15:50, out 16:12. The letter invited her for 16:00.
Planning-office minutes: meeting 15:00–17:00, K. Mutisya presenting.
Imran: his mother refused every offer for the building. "Auntie Yasmin needs money. Everyone knows." Yasmin never had a share of the shop itself.
Imran is in a Nairobi hotel on business; he took the video call from its lobby.
Rahma: "I was in the shop all afternoon. Nobody came."
Rahma admits she slipped out at 15:35 for a job interview in Nyali and left the "back shortly" sign. Farida didn't know.
Yasmin: "That building is half mine. She was sentimental."
Ken: "I was presenting at the county planning office."
Ken admits he told Farida "you'll sell, one way or another". "I meant the courts. Developers sue. They don't kill."

interrogations.intro: Rahma sits on a sack of chillies, her good blouse dusted yellow. "I was here. I was here all afternoon."

topics.reply: Auntie Yasmin? She comes sometimes. They argue about the building. In Gujarati, so I don't understand.

interrogations.intro: Yasmin opens her door a hand's width. "I have heard. I am in mourning. What do you want?"

topics.reply: Half mine. Forty million, and she wanted to sit on it selling cloves.
Silence. She looks at the rack for a long time and says nothing at all.

interrogations.intro: Ken Mutisya steps out of a meeting to take the call. "Mrs Karimjee? I'm very sorry. What does this have to do with me?"

topics.reply: One way or another, I said. I meant the courts. Developers sue. We don't kill people.

interrogations.intro: Imran, on a video call from a Nairobi hotel lobby, keeps his hand over his mouth. "Mummy. Mummy."

topics.reply: Mummy refused every offer. Auntie Yasmin needs money, everyone knows. But she never had any share of the shop. Only the building.

interrogations.intro: Ali Kitsao answers from his tuk-tuk at a Ganjoni stage. "Two fares from that number? Yes. The lady in white."
Hussein wipes sawdust from his hands. "Thirty years I carve doors on this pavement. I see every door on Ndia Kuu."

topics.reply: The girl put a sign up and went off at twenty-five to four, in her best clothes. I thought: a boy.

contradictions.reaction: I went for an interview. A hotel in Nyali. Mama didn't know. I left the sign. I only wanted a job with a pension. I'm so sorry. I'm so sorry.

words.text: Farida refused to sell the family building
she'd been cut out of the spice business
she caught her stealing from the till

prosecutor.pass: Saa tisa na nusu, a tuk-tuk to the door, and turmeric that doesn't wash out. That will hold.
fail: Doesn't hold up. The girl lied to hide a job interview. Who walked through that unattended door?
No. A developer who threatens in public sues in private. Who was in the shop?

prosecutor.pass: Forty million and one word written across it. The why is in her handwriting.
fail: She did it, but not for that. Read the trust deed: what needed two signatures?
That's someone else's grievance, or none at all.

proof.concludes: Rahma said she never left, but the sign was up from 15:35 and nothing was sold until 16:25; she was in a hotel in Nyali from 15:50 to 16:12. The shop was unattended. Her lie hid a job hunt, not a crime.

Yasmin texted that she was coming at half past three with papers. Her phone was in Old Town from 15:42 to 16:14, and the tuk-tuk she paid dropped her at the shop door at 15:47 and collected her at 16:12.
Turmeric from the split sack is on Yasmin's dupatta, and the transfer form she brought is torn in the bin. The sale needed Farida's signature, and Farida wrote NEVER. Yasmin Karimjee killed her.

eliminations.why: Ken was presenting at the county planning office from 15:00 to 17:00.
Rahma was at a hotel in Nyali from 15:50 to 16:12.
Hussein carved at his pavement workshop across the street all afternoon.
The old family loan was settled ten years ago.
The trust covers only the building. Yasmin never had a share of the shop to be cut out of.
That is Ken's pressure, not Yasmin's reason, and Ken was in a meeting.

reconstruction.text: A developer offers forty million for the building. Farida writes NEVER across the letter. A sale needs both signatures.
Three days earlier, Yasmin pays Mvua Holdings for "transfer documents". At 14:58 she texts: coming at half past three, with papers.
15:35. Rahma slips out for a job interview and hangs "back shortly" on the door. At 15:47 a tuk-tuk drops Yasmin there.
Farida tears up the papers. The pestle. In the struggle the turmeric sack splits, over the floor, over a white dupatta, over flat sandals.
16:12. The same tuk-tuk takes her home to Ganjoni. That evening she washes the dupatta. Turmeric doesn't wash out.

tier1.line: Someone said they were coming at saa tisa na nusu. In Swahili time, hours start at six in the morning. Do the sum.

tier2.line: Turmeric stains cotton and won't wash out. Whose white cloth is drying today?

tier1.line: What needed two signatures, and who wouldn't give hers?

tier2.line: Forty million on the table, and one word written across it.

glossary.def: Nine o'clock in Swahili time, which counts the hours from 6 am: 3 pm. "Saa tisa na nusu": half past three.
A long scarf worn with a salwar suit.
Mother; also a respectful way to address or name a woman.
Fictional mobile-money service used in the game.

ui.beatNotes: Language as evidence: an SMS in Swahili with a tap-to-translate toggle. "Saa tisa na nusu" is 15:30 in Swahili time-telling (hours count from 06:00); the glossary explains it and the toggle shows "3:30 pm".
